title: Amazon Orders 2 Million More Nvidia Chips in Tens-of-Billions AI Expansion
excerpt: AWS will deploy Nvidia's next-generation Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra GPUs through 2028, as Amazon pursues a dual strategy of building its own chips while deepening ties with Nvidia.
body:
• Amazon has ordered 2 million additional Nvidia GPU chips — Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra — for AWS data centers through 2028, in a deal worth tens of billions of dollars.
  • The order comes five months after Amazon committed to deploying over 1 million Nvidia GPUs, signaling relentless demand for AI compute capacity.
  • Amazon is simultaneously building its own custom silicon — Trainium and Graviton — which already generates $25 billion in annualized revenue.
  • Nvidia reported Q2 revenue of $96.2 billion with data center revenue up 117% year-over-year, and guided Q3 to $108 billion.

A Deal Measured in Millions of Chips

Amazon and Nvidia announced an expanded partnership that will bring 2 million additional Nvidia GPU chips to Amazon Web Services data centers between 2027 and 2028. The order spans Nvidia's next-generation Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra architectures — chips that have not yet shipped at scale.

Neither company disclosed financial terms, but analysts estimate the deal is worth tens of billions of dollars. It arrives just five months after Amazon agreed to deploy more than 1 million Nvidia GPUs across AWS, making the cumulative commitment one of the largest chip procurement deals in computing history.

Beyond GPUs, the partnership extends across Nvidia's full product stack. AWS will integrate Nvidia's Vera CPUs, networking hardware, and its robotics platform — including Omniverse, Cosmos, Isaac, and Jetson — into cloud and warehouse operations. Amazon plans to use Nvidia's physical AI stack to power robots across its fulfillment centers.

"AI is generating profitable tokens... everybody's leaning in."

— Jensen Huang, CEO, Nvidia

Amazon's Dual Silicon Strategy

The massive Nvidia order does not mean Amazon is abandoning its own chip ambitions. The company continues to develop Trainium AI training chips and Graviton general-purpose processors, a custom silicon business that now generates $25 billion in annualized revenue, according to Amazon.

The dual strategy reflects a pragmatic calculation: demand for AI compute is growing faster than any single supplier can fill. By investing in both Nvidia's GPUs and its own custom chips, Amazon hedges against supply constraints while offering AWS customers a broader range of price and performance options.

AWS will also serve Nvidia's Nemotron family of models on Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker, giving enterprise customers access to Nvidia's AI software alongside its hardware.

Nvidia's Commanding Position

The Amazon deal underscores Nvidia's grip on the AI infrastructure market. The company reported fiscal Q2 revenue of $96.2 billion, beating Wall Street estimates, with data center revenue reaching $89 billion — up 117% year-over-year. Nvidia guided third-quarter revenue to $108 billion.

Supply commitments from cloud providers and enterprises surged to $279 billion, more than doubling from $119 billion the previous quarter. Nvidia said production shipments of its Rubin architecture have already begun.

"Vera CPUs will be deployed by every major hyperscaler."

— Colette Kress, CFO, Nvidia

The numbers paint a picture of an industry where spending on AI infrastructure continues to accelerate despite periodic debates about whether returns justify the investment. With Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta all expanding GPU fleets, Nvidia's order book suggests the buildout is far from peaking.

What It Means for the AI Arms Race

Amazon's order is the latest in a series of enormous compute deals that have defined 2026. Anthropic recently signed a $45 billion compute agreement. SpaceX committed $1.25 billion per month across two data centers. Microsoft, Google, and Meta have each announced multi-billion-dollar infrastructure expansions.

For Amazon, the Nvidia partnership is a bet that enterprise AI workloads will continue migrating to the cloud at scale. For Nvidia, it is confirmation that even customers building competing chips still need its GPUs in massive quantities. The 2-million-chip order sets a new benchmark for what AI-scale procurement looks like.
